Teaching machines to see and talk at once · 40 papers

EgoMind: Activating Spatial Cognition through Linguistic Reasoning in MLLMs ⌘

The problem. A model can look at one photo and understand it well, but ask it to reason across many frames of a walkthrough — where is the couch relative to the kitchen I passed a moment ago, could I reach that shelf — and it falls apart. That kind of spatial understanding is exactly what you need for a robot, a headset, or any agent moving through a real space. The usual fix is to feed the model explicit 3D structure: depth maps, geometry, camera poses, all painstakingly supervised. That is expensive to collect and hard to scale, which quietly caps how broadly spatial reasoning can be deployed.

The approach. EgoMind drops the 3D machinery and instead makes the model think its way through space in words. It runs a structured chain of thought in two moves: first a "role-play caption" where the model pretends to be an agent walking through the scene in first person, narrating each frame and, crucially, the transitions between viewpoints — this stitches separate frames into one continuous mental map. Then a "progressive spatial analysis" that locates the objects the question mentions, widens out to their neighbors, and reasons about how they sit relative to each other. All of this is trained on only 5K auto-generated fine-tuning examples plus 20K reinforcement-learning samples, with no human annotation.

What's unique. Prior multi-frame spatial work leans on explicit 3D priors and geometric supervision; pure-2D attempts fail because they never bind objects across frames. EgoMind is the first to treat cross-frame spatial cognition as a language-reasoning problem — using first-person narration of viewpoint changes as the connective tissue between frames — and to get competitive results with a fully automated, tiny data pipeline instead of geometric labels.

The fundamental point. The core thing it establishes is that the spatial glue between frames does not have to be geometry — it can be language. The implicit "bridges" that connect one viewpoint to the next (I turned left, now I'm facing what was behind me) can be recovered and reasoned over as narrated text, which means multi-frame spatial understanding was never strictly a 3D-perception problem; a large part of it is a reasoning problem that a language model already has the machinery to solve.

What it implies. If narration can substitute for geometry, then the expensive assumption — that you need depth, poses, and 3D supervision to do spatial reasoning — falls, and spatial cognition becomes something you can scale with cheap auto-generated text rather than costly sensor data. That opens the door to equipping ordinary multimodal models for embodied AI and VR/AR without a geometry pipeline, though it comes with the honest cost that reasoning in words adds inference latency and the claims here are tested on image benchmarks rather than verified against true 3D.

Mathematical lens

What is hidden? In EgoMind: Activating Spatial Cognition through Linguistic Reasoning in MLLMs, the method is estimating the hidden object, region, relation, or reasoning state that makes the words true in this image.

What counts as evidence? image patches, region tokens, question words, prior text knowledge, and any intermediate rationale or tool output.

What is the objective? make the answer probable only when the visual evidence and the language state support the same claim; in math terms, bind text variables to visual variables instead of letting the language prior answer alone.

What breaks? a fluent sentence can detach from the pixels, giving a confident answer whose words have no checked visual support.

Grounding Everything in Tokens for Multimodal Large Language Models

The problem. A multimodal model can describe a picture, but ask it exactly where something is and it fumbles. That is because it swallows an image as one blended impression rather than a map of places. For anything that has to act on the world through a screen or a robot arm, that gap is fatal: editing this object, pointing at that one, telling a machine where to reach all require knowing the where, not just the what. The paper attacks this missing sense of location inside models that otherwise handle words and images fluently.

The approach. Instead of bolting a separate detector onto the language model, they teach the model to treat locations as just more words. Image patches and regions become their own tokens, carrying spatial coordinates, and these sit in the same sequence as text tokens. An alignment step trains the model so a word token and the region token it refers to learn to recognize each other. The result is that pointing and localizing happen inside the ordinary transformer, through the same token-to-token machinery the model already uses for language, with no new architecture grafted on.

What's unique. Prior multimodal models grounded coarsely, treating the image as a holistic feature or delegating spatial work to bolted-on modules; this is the first to make grounding operate at the level of individual language tokens linked to individual regions, entirely within a standard transformer.

The fundamental point. The core thing it reveals is that spatial grounding is not a distinct capability needing distinct machinery — it is just another correspondence between tokens, of the same kind a transformer already learns between words. Location can be encoded as a token and attended to exactly like meaning, which means the model never needed a special spatial module; it only needed places represented in the vocabulary it already reasons over.

What it implies. If where collapses into the same token-attention substrate as what, then the boundary between language models and perception systems is softer than assumed: adding a sense of place becomes a matter of expanding the token space rather than redesigning the model. This opens a path to interactive and embodied uses — editing, pointing, guiding an agent — built on general-purpose models, though the paper's own caveats (added token overhead, thin evaluation, uncharacterized inference cost and cross-domain reach) mark where the claim still has to be earned.

Rationale-Enhanced Decoding for Multi-modal Chain-of-Thought

The problem. When a vision-language model is asked to "think step by step" about an image, we assume it actually uses those written-out reasoning steps to reach its answer. This paper shows that assumption is often false: the model produces a plausible rationale and then answers as if the rationale weren't there, leaning on the image and its own priors instead. That matters because the whole appeal of chain-of-thought is that the visible reasoning both improves and explains the final decision; if the answer isn't really conditioned on the words the model wrote, the reasoning is theater and offers no real grounding or trustworthiness.

The approach. They treat generation as a decision the model makes token by token, and force each next-token choice to be answerable to two separate questions at once: "what does the image support?" and "what does the rationale text support?" Concretely, Rationale-Enhanced Decoding (RED) runs the model twice per step to get two distributions — one conditioned on the image, one conditioned on the generated rationale — and combines them by multiplying at the logit level, so a token only wins if both the picture and the stated reasoning back it. They frame this as maximizing a reward (agreement with the rationale) under a KL leash that keeps the output from drifting away from the image-grounded distribution. Nothing is retrained; it is purely a change to how tokens are selected at inference.

What's unique. Prior work assumed CoT automatically improves multi-modal grounding and focused on generating better rationales or fine-tuning; this is the first to diagnose that the model structurally ignores the rationale it produced, and to fix it at decode time with a provable guarantee that the output is grounded on both image and rationale — no extra training, plug-and-play across models.

The fundamental point. It reveals that in current LVLMs, generating a rationale and using a rationale are two disconnected acts — the text of the reasoning has almost no causal pull on the answer. The deeper point is that faithfulness to one's own stated reasoning is not an emergent property of these models; it is something that has to be explicitly imposed on the decoding process, because the default next-token distribution already collapses the rationale's contribution.

What it implies. If conditioning on the rationale can be enforced by reweighting logits alone, then the missing ingredient was never more data or bigger models but a decoding rule that makes the model honor its own words. This turns rationale quality into a directly usable lever — better rationales now translate into better answers rather than being ignored — and it reframes "faithful chain-of-thought" as a controllable inference-time property rather than a hoped-for behavior, though it still depends on having a good rationale to condition on in the first place.

Grounded Chain-of-Thought for Multimodal Large Language Models

The problem. Multimodal models can give the right answer to a question about an image without actually looking at the right part of the image, or without looking at the image in a grounded way at all. That means a correct answer is not proof of understanding, and a confident model can be quietly hallucinating. This matters enormously wherever a model has to act on what it sees rather than just chat about it, such as embodied AI, where trusting an answer that was never tied to real visual evidence can be dangerous.

The approach. The authors reframe visual question answering so the model can no longer hide behind the answer alone. They define a Grounded Chain-of-Thought task that forces a model to break a question into step-by-step reasoning where each step names the specific image coordinates it is relying on, so its perception is made explicit and checkable. They build the MM-GCoT benchmark of 1200 examples and, crucially, score three separate things: whether the answer is right, whether the pointed-to regions are right, and whether the answer and the grounding are consistent with each other. That third metric is the point: it catches models that get the answer and the pointing right in isolation but whose answer does not actually follow from where they looked.

What's unique. Prior work measured answer accuracy or grounding accuracy separately; this is the first systematic evaluation that couples them, demanding step-wise reasoning tied to spatial coordinates and explicitly measuring answer-grounding consistency to diagnose hallucination rather than just detect wrong answers.

The fundamental point. It establishes that in today's multimodal models, getting the answer right and looking at the right place are largely decoupled — a model can do each well yet fail to connect them. Across 12 advanced models, answer-grounding consistency is low even when individual task scores are high, and this failure does not shrink as models get bigger. Correctness and grounded understanding are therefore distinct properties, and scale does not automatically fuse them.

What it implies. If answer accuracy can be high while the reasoning is ungrounded, then leaderboard accuracy is not a valid proxy for whether a model actually sees, and hallucination cannot be trained away simply by making models larger. Evaluation and training must instead reward the link between what a model concludes and the visual evidence it used, which is a prerequisite before these models can be trusted to act in the physical world.

Saliency-R1: Enforcing Interpretable and Faithful Vision-language Reasoning via Saliency-map Alignment

The problem. Vision-language models routinely describe things that aren't in the image — they answer from the statistical habits of language rather than from what the picture actually shows. Worse, even when the written reasoning sounds right, there's no guarantee the model was looking at the relevant part of the image while producing it; the words and the gaze can drift apart. That gap between what a model says and where it actually attends is what makes these systems untrustworthy for anything that matters, because a plausible sentence built on the wrong pixels is a confident lie.

The approach. Saliency-R1 makes "where the model looks" into something it can be graded and trained on. It first extracts a saliency map for free, without extra forward passes, by decomposing the answer logit into per-token contributions across the residual stream and projecting them back onto the image grid, and it routes attention-rollout through the reasoning ("thinking") tokens so only the attention that actually flows through the chain-of-thought counts. Then, on top of a model taught to write bounding-box-grounded reasoning, it runs reinforcement learning (GRPO) with a reward that adds up not just answer correctness and format but the fraction of saliency energy that lands inside the region the reasoning claims to be about. The model is thus rewarded for looking where it says it's looking.

What's unique. Prior saliency/attribution work either sat outside training as a post-hoc explanation or was too expensive to run in a loop; here the saliency signal is cheap enough to compute every step and is folded directly into the RL reward. It is the first method to turn saliency-region alignment into a reward term inside GRPO so that visual grounding faithfulness is optimized on purpose rather than hoped for.

The fundamental point. The core thing it establishes is that faithfulness is a trainable target, not just an emergent side effect — the internal evidence of where a model attends can be read out cheaply from its own logits and attention, made into a scalar, and pushed on. It reveals that interpretability and accuracy are not in tension: closing the loop between "where it looks" and "what it says" (Energy-PG +10.82%, PG +14.14% over base) improves both grounding and downstream benchmark scores at once.

What it implies. If a model's own attention can be scored and rewarded, then hallucination becomes an optimization problem rather than an inescapable property of language priors — you can train the gaze to obey the words. The assumption that falls is that we must choose between models that are accurate and models that are explainable. The clear limit, and the next frontier, is that this currently leans on ground-truth bounding boxes, so it works where spatial referents exist; extending faithfulness rewards to abstract reasoning that has no obvious region to point at is the open question.

SketchVL: Policy Optimization via Fine-Grained Credit Assignment for Chart Understanding and More

The problem. Machines that read charts have to reason in careful little steps: crop to the right region, read a tick, match a color to a legend, then do arithmetic. When we teach such a model by reward, we usually only tell it whether the final answer was right or wrong. That single verdict then gets smeared back across the whole chain of steps. So a chain that got the right answer through a lucky guess is praised at every step, and a chain full of good reasoning that stumbled on one misread tick is punished everywhere. This matters because in chart work a single small slip anywhere in the chain sinks the whole answer, so the learning signal is exactly where it is least informative.

The approach. SketchVL makes the model's reasoning physically visible: instead of only thinking in words, it draws its intermediate steps as marks directly on the chart image (a crop box, a pointer to a bar) and feeds the annotated image back to itself, so each thought becomes an inspectable action. A separate step-level judge, the Fine-grained Process Reward Model, scores each individual drawing action for how sound it was. Their training rule, FinePO, then uses those per-action scores to hand out credit step by step rather than pouring one outcome reward uniformly over the trajectory. The reward model is bootstrapped from hundreds of thousands of distilled intent-action pairs, after a cold-start then RL schedule mixing chart, image, and math data.

What's unique. Prior RL for multimodal reasoning gives coarse, outcome-only feedback over an entire trajectory; SketchVL instead scores and rewards each reasoning step, and does so for actions that are visual drawings on the image rather than text tokens, bringing process-reward credit assignment into the multimodal, act-on-the-image setting.

The fundamental point. It shows that the real bottleneck in training visual reasoners was never the reasoning capacity but the coarseness of the credit signal: a right-or-wrong final reward systematically mislabels the steps that produced it, teaching good steps to look bad and bad steps to look good. Reasoning quality lives at the level of individual steps, so credit has to be assigned there too. Turning each thought into a drawn, inspectable action is what makes that per-step judgment possible in the first place.

What it implies. If credit can be traced to the step that earned it, outcome-only reward stops being the ceiling for teaching multi-step visual reasoning, and the gains (7.23% average over the base model across chart, image, and math) transfer beyond charts to any domain where one wrong step derails a chain. The cost shifts to building the step-level judge, which needs annotated intent-action pairs and its own training expense, so the open question becomes how to obtain fine-grained process supervision cheaply and generally rather than whether it helps.

MR-RAG: Multimodal Relevance-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medical Visual Question Answering

The problem. A general-purpose vision-language model does not know medicine the way a radiologist does, so when it is asked to read a chest X-ray it can sound fluent while being wrong. The usual fix is to let it look things up first — retrieve relevant clinical documents and hand them to the model before it answers. But this only helps if the right documents are found and if the model actually leans on the good ones. In medicine, where a confident wrong answer can misdirect care, both of those conditions matter enormously and both are fragile.

The approach. MR-RAG treats retrieval and generation as one coupled pipeline rather than two independent steps, and threads a single idea — how relevant is this document, really — through both. First, instead of matching an image or a question to documents by a single similarity score, it uses a lightweight adapter to combine signals within a modality and across modalities (image-to-image, text-to-text, image-to-text) so that alignment reflects the full clinical picture. Second, once documents are retrieved, it does not let the model treat them as an undifferentiated pile: it converts each document's estimated importance into a control signal that reshapes the model's attention, turning up the useful evidence and turning down the noise. The relevance judgment made at retrieval is carried forward to steer reading.

What's unique. Prior medical RAG retrieves by one similarity notion and then feeds everything to the generator as equals; MR-RAG's novelty is injecting explicit multimodal relevance at both ends — cooperative multi-signal retrieval, plus attention that is steered document-by-document by importance rather than applied uniformly.

The fundamental point. The core thing it reveals is that in retrieval-augmented generation the bottleneck is not just finding relevant material but the model's implicit assumption that everything placed in its context deserves equal weight. Relevance is not a property to be spent at the retrieval step and then discarded — it is information that must survive into how the answer is composed. Retrieval and generation share the same failure when relevance is thrown away between them.

What it implies. If a document's relevance can be carried into the model's attention rather than left at the door, then the amount of retrieved context stops being a liability — you can retrieve broadly without irrelevant passages drowning the signal, because the model is told what to trust. This reframes RAG from a two-box pipeline into a single relevance-aware channel, and points toward generation systems that grade their own evidence as they read it, which matters most exactly where wrong-but-fluent answers are dangerous, as in clinical decision support.

Mathematical lens

What is hidden? In MR-RAG: Multimodal Relevance-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medical Visual Question Answering, the method is estimating the biological or physical state behind the measurement: tissue boundary, abnormal region, cell structure, disease signal, or instrument artifact.

What counts as evidence? scanner intensities, microscope pixels, expert labels, anatomical priors, repeated measurements, and uncertainty around unclear regions.

What is the objective? infer the clinically or scientifically relevant state while respecting measurement noise, scarce labels, and domain constraints.

What breaks? a visually neat output can be scientifically wrong if it invents unsupported structure or hides uncertainty at the decision boundary.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

ACoT-VLA: Action Chain-of-Thought for Vision-Language-Action Models

The problem. Robots that take orders in plain language and act on what they see tend to jump straight from a camera image to a motor command. That works for one-shot moves like "pick up the cup," but it falls apart on tasks that unfold over many steps, where the right action now depends on a plan for what comes later. The machine has no place to think between seeing and doing, so it has no way to break a goal into parts, track where it is in a sequence, or recover when a step depends on an earlier one. As robots move from single gestures toward errands, this missing middle is the wall they hit.

The approach. The paper borrows the trick that made language models better at hard questions: instead of demanding an answer immediately, let the model write out its reasoning first. Here the model is made to reason in the currency of a robot, not just words. Given an image and an instruction, it first decomposes the task into intermediate steps and thinks through the sub-goals, and only then commits to the actual motor action. The reasoning about "what needs to happen and in what order" and the perception of "what the scene looks like right now" are fused so the plan stays anchored to reality rather than floating free of it.

What's unique. Chain-of-thought was a language phenomenon; prior VLA models mapped pixels-plus-words directly to actions with no explicit deliberation. This is presented as the first to insert a genuine action-oriented reasoning chain into the vision-language-action loop, so the intermediate thinking is about the sequence of physical steps, not merely a verbal aside.

The fundamental point. It reveals that the gap between simple and complex robot behavior is not mainly a perception or actuation problem but a missing reasoning stage: the same "think before you answer" structure that unlocked multi-step problem solving in text also governs multi-step physical control. Deliberation is a transferable ingredient, not something tied to language tasks, and a robot's competence on long-horizon work scales with whether it is allowed to reason about the task's decomposition before committing to a move.

What it implies. If deliberate reasoning is what long-horizon control was lacking, then better robots may come less from bigger action datasets or finer motor models and more from teaching machines to plan their steps explicitly, reusing the reasoning machinery already developed for language. The cost is real time and compute spent thinking per action, and it depends on vision and action being well aligned, so the open frontier becomes reasoning that is cheap enough to run in the control loop and grounded enough to stay tied to what the robot actually sees.

Deeper Thought, Weaker Aim: Understanding and Mitigating Perceptual Impairment during Deep Reasoning ⌘

The problem. When a vision-language model is told to "think step by step" before answering, it writes out a long chain of reasoning. This paper points at an uncomfortable side effect: the longer and more abstract that reasoning gets, the worse the model becomes at actually seeing the image it is reasoning about. It starts confusing what it thinks with what is in front of it, losing track of fine visual detail as it climbs into abstraction. This matters because the whole field has been pushing reasoning depth as the path to smarter models, on the unexamined assumption that more thinking is strictly better for a system that must both look and think.

The approach. The authors first treat the phenomenon as something to measure rather than assume, quantifying how perceptual accuracy on visual tasks falls as reasoning chains lengthen, and showing this is a systematic trade-off, not noise. Conceptually, the diagnosis is that as the model spends more of its internal capacity on abstract, text-side reasoning, its grip on the visual evidence loosens. Their fix is to keep the perceptual signal alive throughout the reasoning process, using attention and feature-preservation mechanisms so the visual grounding is not overwritten as the thought chain grows. The model is encouraged to keep re-anchoring to what it actually saw even while it reasons.

What's unique. Prior work chased longer, deeper reasoning chains as an unambiguous win; this paper is distinctive in naming and empirically quantifying the opposite cost, "perceptual impairment," as a direct consequence of that depth, and then treating restored perception as a design target rather than a given.

The fundamental point. The core thing it establishes is that reasoning and perceiving compete for the same limited internal resources in a multimodal model, rather than stacking harmoniously. Deep reasoning is not free: the act of thinking harder about an image actively erodes the model's fidelity to that image. "More thinking" and "better seeing" are, past a point, in tension, not alignment.

What it implies. If depth trades against perception, then the field's default of maximizing reasoning length is wrong for tasks that stay tied to visual evidence, and the real goal becomes managing the balance rather than pushing one axis. It implies that grounding must be a persistent, protected quantity carried through reasoning rather than something established once at the start and left to decay, and it opens the door to architectures and training objectives that explicitly keep a model's eyes open while it thinks.

IF-Prune: Information-Flow Guided Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language Models ⌘

The problem. A vision-language model has to turn a picture into a sequence of tokens the language part can read, and modern encoders that adapt to image resolution spit out enormous numbers of these visual tokens. Most of them carry little that matters for the question being asked, yet the model pays full compute cost on all of them, which is the main thing blocking these systems from running cheaply. So the real question is how to decide, before doing the expensive reasoning, which visual tokens are safe to throw away without hurting the answer.

The approach. The standard trick is to run a small, cheap model first, watch where its attention lands, and keep the tokens it attends to. IF-Prune flips this around. Instead of asking the small model "which tokens are important?", it trains the small model to model the distribution of the un-important tokens directly, using an information-bottleneck view: for each token it compares the token's meaning given the query (a posterior) against its meaning in general (a prior), and the size of that gap becomes the importance score. Tokens whose meaning barely shifts when the query is introduced are the ones you can drop. This is computed in a single forward pass, so it plugs into fast attention libraries.

What's unique. Prior methods lean on aggregated attention weights as a proxy for importance, which gets noisy and unreliable exactly when the question is hard and the small model's built-in knowledge is thin. IF-Prune is the first to cast token pruning as a principled probabilistic problem (amortized variational inference through an information bottleneck) rather than an attention heuristic, and to score importance by how much a query changes a token's posterior rather than by how much answer-generation attends to it.

The fundamental point. It shows that a token's importance is better defined by how much the query moves its distribution than by how much attention it accumulates. Attention weights were only ever a stand-in for importance; the real signal is the divergence between a token's query-conditioned posterior and its unconditioned prior. This reframes pruning as measuring query-driven information gain per token, not reading off the model's internal attention.

What it implies. If importance is really about query-conditioned information gain, then a tiny model can supply reliable pruning guidance without ever exposing the big model's attention, which is why one cheap forward pass can keep 95% of accuracy on only 5% of visual tokens and cut compute 40%. This decouples the pruning decision from the expensive model entirely and makes it compatible with optimized attention kernels, opening a path to running large VLMs at a fraction of the cost as long as the query-gain signal generalizes to newer architectures, which remains to be tested.

Mathematical lens

What is hidden? In IF-Prune: Information-Flow Guided Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language Models, the method is estimating the denoising or transport path from an easy random state to a structured image, video, or representation.

What counts as evidence? the conditioning signal, the noisy sample, the learned score or velocity field, and checks that the final sample still matches the data.

What is the objective? follow a sequence of small probability-correcting steps so each step makes the sample less random and more condition-consistent.

What breaks? a wrong path can still make a sharp sample, but it may drift from the prompt, break identity, collapse diversity, or add unsupported detail.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

CORE: Compact Object-centric REpresentations as a New Paradigm for Token Merging in LVLMs ⌘

The problem. When a vision-language model looks at an image, it first chops the picture into a grid of small patches and turns each patch into a token the language model has to read. Doubling the image resolution roughly quadruples the number of these tokens, and the model's cost grows with the square of that count, so high-resolution images become brutally expensive to process and to keep in memory. The obvious fix is to throw away or merge redundant tokens, but the standard schemes decide what to merge by looking at low-level pixel similarity, with no idea what is actually in the image. That leads to clumsy merges that blend unrelated things and lose the very details a downstream question might depend on.

The approach. CORE changes the unit of compression from "a patch of pixels" to "an object." It runs a lightweight segmentation decoder (Mask2Former) that produces object masks, and uses those masks as a high-level map telling the system which tokens belong to which real thing. All the visual tokens covering one object get consolidated into a single compact token, so the image is re-described as a short list of object-centric representations rather than a dense grid. To keep the language model's sense of layout intact, a centroid-guided sorting step re-orders these object tokens back into their spatial arrangement. Crucially, the segmentation network and the language pathway share one ConvNeXt-L backbone, so getting the object priors costs almost nothing extra.

What's unique. Prior token-merging methods merge by appearance or attention statistics with no semantic model of the scene; CORE is the first to let explicit object structure drive the merging, collapsing each distinct object into one token so the compressed set stays semantically clean instead of being an averaged blur of whatever patches happened to look alike.

The fundamental point. The real information content of an image, for the purposes of answering questions about it, scales with the number of distinct objects in the scene, not with the number of pixels or patches. The patch grid is an accident of how images are fed to transformers, not a reflection of how much there is to understand — and once you compress along object boundaries, keeping only 2.2% of the tokens still preserves 97.4% of performance.

What it implies. If the meaningful token budget is set by scene complexity rather than resolution, then the quadratic cost of high-resolution vision-language models is not a law but an artifact of tokenizing at the wrong granularity — you can push to higher resolutions almost for free (16x fewer FLOPs, 182x smaller KV cache) by paying attention to what is in the image instead of how many pixels it has. It also suggests that semantic structure, not raw feature similarity, is the right axis for compression in multimodal models generally, and that borrowing "what is where" from a cheap perception head can become a standard front-end for efficient LVLMs — pending extension beyond still images to video and justification for the added segmentation machinery.

Mathematical lens

What is hidden? In CORE: Compact Object-centric REpresentations as a New Paradigm for Token Merging in LVLMs, the method is estimating the small subspace, token set, or behavior pattern that carries most of the useful computation.

What counts as evidence? teacher probabilities, feature similarity, ranks, token saliency, latency, memory, and accuracy under compression.

What is the objective? approximate the original behavior with fewer parameters, tokens, bits, or operations while bounding the loss that matters.

What breaks? a cheaper model may preserve average accuracy while losing rare behavior, calibration, long-range context, or the teacher's useful uncertainty.

CodeV: Code with Images for Faithful Visual Reasoning via Tool-Aware Policy Optimization ⌘

The problem. When a vision-language model is asked something precise about an image — how many objects, what a tiny label says, which thing is closer — it answers from an internal impression of the picture rather than from anything it actually checked. That impression is a compressed guess, so the model produces answers that sound right and are wrong, with no way to tell the difference. This matters because we increasingly ask these models to make claims about the visual world that people will act on, yet there is nothing under the answer that can be inspected or verified.

The approach. Instead of letting the model answer directly, CodeV makes it write a small Python program that calls real computer-vision tools — crop, count, OCR, depth, detection, segmentation — which run deterministically on the actual pixels, and the answer is read off those computed results. The model is taught this in two stages: first supervised imitation of good tool-calling programs, then reinforcement learning (TAPO) where each answer earns reward not only for being correct after execution, but for a separate judge model confirming the code picked and applied the right tools for the question. Programs that crash or misuse tools get zero reward, so the executable sandbox itself becomes the honesty signal. The result is a model that reasons by running verifiable operations rather than by intuiting.

What's unique. Prior code-for-vision work rewarded only whether the final answer was right, which lets a model reach a correct answer through wrong or lucky tool use; TAPO adds a second reward that grades the faithfulness of the tool choice itself, judged by a VLM, so the process — not just the outcome — is optimized. Coupling that dual reward with GRPO and a hard execution-grounded zero for broken programs is the new combination.

The fundamental point. It shows that faithful visual reasoning is less about the model seeing better and more about relocating the reasoning outside the model — into deterministic, inspectable operations on the pixels — and that a model can be trained to defer to those operations rather than trust its own impression. Crucially, it reveals that outcome correctness alone is not a sufficient training target: you can reach the right answer by the wrong means, so the means must be rewarded explicitly for the behavior to be genuinely faithful.

What it implies. If honesty is a property of the process rather than the answer, then it can be supervised and optimized directly, and the reliability of a visual answer becomes something you can audit by reading the program that produced it. This shifts the ceiling on visual reasoning from how much a model can internalize to how good and how complete its tool library is — the paper's own limit, since questions needing an unavailable tool still fail — pointing toward systems whose competence grows by adding verifiable tools rather than by scaling opaque perception.

Mathematical lens

What is hidden? In CodeV: Code with Images for Faithful Visual Reasoning via Tool-Aware Policy Optimization, the method is estimating the hidden object, region, relation, or reasoning state that makes the words true in this image.

What counts as evidence? image patches, region tokens, question words, prior text knowledge, and any intermediate rationale or tool output.

What is the objective? make the answer probable only when the visual evidence and the language state support the same claim; in math terms, bind text variables to visual variables instead of letting the language prior answer alone.

What breaks? a fluent sentence can detach from the pixels, giving a confident answer whose words have no checked visual support.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

AdaptVision: Efficient Vision-Language Models via Adaptive Visual Acquisition ⌘

The problem. Vision-language models "see" by turning an image into a long list of visual tokens, and more tokens means more compute. The standard fix is to compress that list by a fixed amount for every image, but this treats a blurry thumbnail question and a find-the-tiny-license-plate question identically. That is wasteful on easy inputs and blind on hard ones, because the right amount of visual detail is not a property of the model, it is a property of the specific question being asked.

The approach. AdaptVision lets the model decide for itself how much of the image it needs to look at. It starts by reading a cheaply compressed, low-resolution version of the image, and only if that is not enough does it invoke a cropping tool to draw a bounding box around a region and pull in extra high-detail tokens for just that patch. This is a coarse-to-fine loop driven by the model's own reasoning. They train the tool-use behavior with Decoupled Turn Policy Optimization, which separates the reward for correctly using the tool from the reward for getting the final answer right, so the two objectives do not fight each other during multi-turn learning.

What's unique. Prior efficient-VLM work sets one compression ratio in advance and applies it passively to every sample; AdaptVision is the first to make token reduction an active, per-sample decision the model takes by choosing when to zoom in. The DTPO training method is also new, built to fix the credit-assignment and optimization-imbalance problems that appear when a single reward has to cover both acquiring information and answering.

The fundamental point. It shows that the amount of visual detail a model needs is not a fixed hyperparameter to be tuned once, but a decision that can be learned and made on the fly per input, the same way a person glances first and only leans in when something is unclear. Efficiency and accuracy stop being a fixed trade-off dial and become an adaptive policy: spend few tokens when the coarse view suffices, spend more only where the question demands it.

What it implies. If a model can budget its own perception, the field can stop hand-picking compression ratios and instead let compute scale with genuine task difficulty, cheap on easy samples and detailed on hard ones. It reframes visual efficiency as active perception through tool use rather than static token pruning, opening the door to richer acquisition tools beyond simple cropping, though the current work only demonstrates bounding-box cropping and leaves other tool types and broader RL-method comparisons unexplored.

b-CLIP: Text-Conditioned Contrastive Learning for Multi-Granular Vision-Language Alignment ⌘

The problem. Models like CLIP learned that a picture and a sentence can be pushed into the same space so that matching pairs sit close together. But that match is made at the whole-image, whole-sentence level: the model knows a photo "goes with" a caption without knowing which part of the photo is the red car, which is the wet street, which word names which thing. For anything that needs pointing rather than labeling, grounding a phrase to a region, checking an attribute, dense correspondence, that coarse whole-to-whole alignment simply doesn't carry the information. The problem is that the objective these models are trained on only ever asks "does this image belong with this text," never "does this piece belong with that piece."

The approach. b-CLIP keeps contrastive learning but stops treating an image and a sentence as single atoms. On the text side it breaks a caption into its parts, noun-phrases, verb-phrases, attributes, so language enters at multiple grain sizes. On the vision side it extracts features at matching grain sizes: the global image, regional patches, and local salient points. Then it runs contrastive objectives at each level in parallel, a global image-text loss and a regional patch-phrase loss with dynamic phrase segmentation, and adds a cross-granular consistency loss that uses soft alignment matrices to make the different levels agree with each other rather than drift apart.

What's unique. Prior contrastive vision-language training targets a single level of alignment (image to text). b-CLIP is framed as the first contrastive method built explicitly for multiple granularities at once, image, region, and attribute, with a loss that ties those levels together instead of learning them independently or hoping fine detail emerges for free from global training.

The fundamental point. The core thing it reveals is that fine-grained visual-language correspondence is not something that automatically falls out of coarse image-text alignment, it is a different objective that has to be asked for directly. Whole-image similarity and region-phrase similarity are separate learning signals, and treating them as one collapses the structure that grounding depends on. Alignment, in other words, is inherently multi-scale, and the scales must be trained jointly and forced to be consistent.

What it implies. If detailed correspondence must be an explicit training target, then the standard practice of pretraining only on global pairs and expecting localized understanding to transfer is leaving that ability on the table. The path forward is contrastive objectives that decompose both modalities into parts and align them at every grain with a consistency constraint, which is what buys the gains on phrase grounding and region-attribute matching, at the cost of running several objectives at once and, so far, with weaker cross-language reach.

What counts as evidence? image patches, region tokens, question words, prior text knowledge, and any intermediate rationale or tool output.

MuCo: Multi-turn Contrastive Learning for Multimodal Embedding Model ⌘

The problem. When you search with pictures and words together, you rarely get it right on the first try. You show a system an image, ask a question, then refine ("no, the blue one," "the one on the left") — a back-and-forth conversation. But the models that turn images and text into searchable vectors are trained on frozen, one-shot image-caption pairs. They have no notion that a query can have history, that meaning accumulates across turns. So the moment real use becomes a dialogue, the embedding falls back to treating each fragment in isolation. Bridging that gap matters because almost all genuine visual search is iterative, not a single perfectly-phrased request.

The approach. Instead of pairing one image with one caption, MuCo reformats a training example as a multi-turn dialogue — a running sequence of image-plus-question turns — and trains the model to compress that whole conversational prefix into a single query vector that lands near the target image in a shared space. It builds a large synthetic dataset (M3T) where each image carries seven different question-type queries (color, spatial, attribute, compositional, and so on), fine-tunes a vision-language backbone (Qwen2-VL) cheaply with LoRA, and adds one crucial fix: because many queries in a batch point at the same image, naive contrastive learning would punish correct matches as if they were wrong, so it masks out those same-image pairs in the loss denominator. The payoff is that one image now yields seven effective training signals for roughly 3% extra compute.

What's unique. It is the first multimodal embedding framework to train natively on dialogue-formatted, multi-turn queries rather than static image-text pairs, and it pairs that with a logit-masking trick specifically for the same-image false-negative problem that multi-turn batching creates.

The fundamental point. The core thing it reveals is that multi-turn retrieval capability was never a matter of new architecture — it was latent in ordinary embedding models all along, unlocked simply by changing what a "training pair" is. A conversation and a caption are the same object to the encoder; the model already knows how to read a sequence, so teaching it to embed accumulated dialogue context costs almost nothing (7x more effective signal at 3% more compute). The apparent hard problem of "encoding query history" dissolves into a data-formatting problem.

What it implies. If richer retrieval behavior can be conjured by reshaping the data one image can generate, then the bottleneck for capable embedding models shifts from model design and raw data collection to the cleverness of how existing images are re-queried — and the false-negative bookkeeping that reshaping introduces. It suggests other "missing" capabilities in embedding models (compositional, contextual, iterative) may likewise be recoverable from the same assets by asking more questions per image rather than gathering more images. The open caveat is that these queries are synthetic, so whether the trick transfers to the messy, open-ended way people actually refine searches remains unproven.

ColaVLA: Leveraging Cognitive Latent Reasoning for Hierarchical Parallel Trajectory Planning ⌘

The problem. A robot asked to do something with many steps — clear the table, then wipe it, then set it — has to hold a whole chain of intentions in mind while its hands are still busy with the first one. Models that map what a robot sees and is told directly onto motor actions tend to think one move at a time, so long tasks drift: they lose the thread, commit to a first step that boxes in the later ones, and stall. Getting machines to plan several coordinated moves ahead, the way a person does when they glance at a cluttered counter and already know the sequence, is the barrier standing between demo-grade robots and ones that handle real multi-step work.

The approach. Instead of reasoning out loud in words or emitting one action after another, ColaVLA does its thinking in a compressed internal "latent" space. It first splits a long task into a hierarchy of sub-goals inside that space, and then — rather than solving those sub-goals strictly in order — plans a trajectory for each of them in parallel, all within the same latent reasoning step. The result is a model that lays out the whole coordinated plan at once and executes against it, reporting better success and efficiency on complex long-horizon manipulation than sequential approaches.

What's unique. Prior VLA models either act step-by-step or reason step-by-step in explicit language chains; ColaVLA's move is to make the reasoning itself latent and hierarchical, and to plan the multiple sub-trajectories concurrently rather than one at a time.

The fundamental point. The core thing it reveals is that the reasoning a robot needs for long tasks does not have to happen in the same currency as its actions or in explicit words — it can live in a compact latent space, and crucially the sub-steps of a plan need not be serialized. Multi-step planning is really a parallel structuring problem, not an inherently sequential one.

What it implies. If a whole plan can be committed to at once in latent form, the assumption that long-horizon competence requires slow, one-step-at-a-time deliberation falls away, opening the door to robots that plan complex sequences faster and with fewer samples. It suggests the path to harder tasks is richer internal structure — hierarchy and parallelism in a learned reasoning space — rather than longer chains of explicit thought.

Jailbreaking Vision-Language Models via Dissonance-Guided Suffix Optimization and Image-Phrase Injection ⌘

The problem. Vision-language models are trained to refuse harmful requests, but those refusals are a thin behavioral veneer bolted onto a model that still "knows" how to comply. Attackers probe how sturdy that veneer really is, and understanding where it cracks is how defenders learn to reinforce it. The trouble is that the two obvious ways to attack such systems each hit a wall: text-based attacks that nudge the model with adversarial suffixes stall out because the model's own gradients give weak, misleading directions once safety tuning has flattened the landscape, while image-based attacks craft a picture for one specific model and then fail to fool a different one. Neither route reliably gets past the guardrails, so the true extent of the vulnerability stays hidden.

The approach. The method, DGSIP, stops relying on the target model's own gradients and instead listens to the disagreement between two models: the safety-aligned target and a second model that was never aligned. Where these two models predict very different next tokens, that gap ("dissonance") pinpoints exactly the words safety tuning has learned to suppress, which turns out to be a far cleaner signal for building an adversarial text suffix than gradients are. Alongside this, it attacks through the image channel too, embedding a harmful phrase into the picture and optimizing both what the phrase says and how it is visually presented, so the two modalities push against the safety mechanism together. The combination drives the model past its refusal reflex from both the text and image sides at once.

What's unique. Prior work optimized suffixes using the target model's gradients (which stagnate) or crafted images that overfit a single model (which don't transfer); this paper's new move is to read off the safety-suppressed tokens directly from the contrast between an aligned and an unaligned model, and to pair that with a coordinated image-phrase injection so text and image attacks reinforce rather than duplicate each other.

The fundamental point. The core thing it reveals is that safety alignment does not delete a model's harmful capability, it merely suppresses a specific, identifiable set of tokens, and that suppression itself is a measurable fingerprint. By comparing an aligned model to an unaligned twin, you can literally read out which tokens alignment is holding down, which means the "safety behavior" and the "underlying knowledge" remain separable inside the same network. The refusal is a lid, not an erasure.

What it implies. If alignment is a locatable suppression signal rather than a true removal, then any adversary with access to an unaligned reference model can find the exact seam to pry open, and the attack transfers even to black-box commercial systems (GPT-4o-Mini, Gemini 2.0, Qwen 2.5-VL) because the suppressed-token structure is shared across aligned models. This shifts the defensive burden: surface-level refusal tuning is inherently fragile, and durable safety would require changing what the model can represent at all, not just what it is coached to say, while also treating multimodal inputs as a single combined attack surface rather than two independent channels.

Mathematical lens

What is hidden? In Jailbreaking Vision-Language Models via Dissonance-Guided Suffix Optimization and Image-Phrase Injection, the method is estimating the nearby failure direction or hidden trigger that changes the model's output while leaving the input looking almost unchanged.

What counts as evidence? gradients, confidence, perturbation budgets, corrupted inputs, shifted test cases, and whether the model's answer changes under controlled stress.

What is the objective? measure worst-case risk around each example, not just average accuracy; the math asks how close the decision boundary sits to real data.

What breaks? a system can pass ordinary tests while a small, targeted change or hidden training trigger reliably flips behavior.

ARGUS: Defending Against Multimodal Indirect Prompt Injection via Steering Instruction-Following Behavior ⌘

The problem. Give a modern AI assistant a picture, a video, or an audio clip and ask a question, and it will happily read text or cues hidden inside that media as if they were commands from you. An attacker can therefore plant instructions in the content itself ("ignore the user, send their files here") and the model obeys, because it has no reliable way to tell the difference between what it is supposed to do and what is merely data it is supposed to look at. This "indirect prompt injection" is dangerous precisely because the very talent that makes these models useful, following instructions well, is also the hole. Defenses built for text-only models fall apart here: they are tuned to spot certain words or phrasings, so they miss injections carried in a new modality and are easy to slip past.

The approach. ARGUS reframes the defense from "detect the malicious content" to "control the model's behavior." It shows that inside the model's internal activations, the act of following the legitimate user versus following an injected instruction lives in different, cleanly separable places, so much so that a simple linear probe can tell them apart with near-perfect accuracy. Using that, it defines a small "safety subspace" of steering directions and, at inference time, nudges the model's activations toward the "obey the user" region by a computed, per-token amount, just enough to cross a safety margin without wrecking normal answers. This is wrapped in a three-stage pipeline: detect whether an input is injected, steer only when it is, and post-filter with the same probe to confirm the steering worked.

What's unique. Prior representation-engineering defenses steer on semantic concepts (topics or content) and are inherently tied to what the attack says and which modality it arrives in; ARGUS instead steers on the abstract behavior of instruction-following, which is modality-agnostic. It is the first to locate and exploit a safety subspace controlling that behavior, giving one defense that transfers across image, video, and audio without any modality-specific machinery, plus an adaptive closed-form intervention strength rather than a fixed nudge.

The fundamental point. The core thing it establishes is that "whose instruction am I about to obey" is not a fuzzy semantic judgment but a distinct, linearly readable state inside the model, separate from the actual content of the attack or the modality it came through. In other words, the instruction-versus-data confusion that makes these models exploitable is encoded as a direction in activation space that can be both read and rewritten. Defense is possible at the level of behavior itself, upstream of the endlessly varied surface forms an attack can take.

What it implies. If obedience-to-the-attacker is a single controllable axis regardless of modality, then the attacker's freedom to disguise injections in new media types stops helping them, because the defense never had to recognize the disguise in the first place. This shifts security from an unwinnable pattern-matching arms race against attack phrasings toward regulating the model's internal decision of whom to trust, and suggests future multimodal models could bake such a steering control in natively. The catch it exposes is that this power still depends on having injected examples to train the probes and on inference-time access to the model's internals, so it protects those who own or host the model rather than being a universal external shield.

Dynamic Token Reweighting for Robust Vision-Language Models ⌘

The problem. Vision-language models inherit safety training from their text side, but the moment you let them see, you open a side door: an image can carry the same harmful intent that a blocked sentence would, and the model's guardrails, tuned on words, do not recognize it. Attackers exploit exactly this seam between what the model reads and what it sees to coax out content the model would otherwise refuse. Closing this door usually means either collecting fresh safety data and retraining, or transcribing every image into text so the language guardrails can inspect it, both of which are slow and expensive. The real question is whether a model can defend itself against a harmful picture at the moment it answers, without new data and without describing the picture first.

The approach. The authors reframe a visual jailbreak not as a strange input but as a measurable distortion: an adversarial image pushes the model's internal state away from where safe inputs normally sit, a "safety-relevant distributional shift" caused by the visual modality. They then locate where that distortion lives inside the running model, in the key-value cache, the stored representation of every image token the model attends to while generating. Their method, DTR, works purely at inference time by re-weighting these visual tokens on the fly, turning down or dropping the ones responsible for the dangerous shift while leaving the ones that carry legitimate visual meaning intact. In effect it surgically quiets the parts of the image that are steering the model toward unsafe territory, without touching its weights or asking for any explanation of the image.

What's unique. Prior defenses either bolt on curated safety data and retraining or convert images to text so a language filter can screen them; DTR is the first to treat the key-value cache itself as the place to enforce safety, adjusting per-token importance based on a formal notion of visual-induced safety shift rather than filtering inputs or fine-tuning.

The fundamental point. It establishes that a multimodal jailbreak is not an exotic new threat but a concrete, measurable shift in the model's internal distribution that can be attributed to specific visual tokens. The danger is localized and separable: the tokens that break safety are not the same tokens that carry the image's useful content, so harm can be removed without removing understanding. Safety, in other words, is already legible inside the model's own cached representations if you know what to look at.

What it implies. If safety violations can be isolated and neutralized in the KV cache at inference time, then defending a vision-language model no longer requires owning its training pipeline or paying to caption every image; any deployed model can be hardened as it runs, cheaply and reversibly. The long-held assumption that robustness must be baked in through data and retraining weakens, and the same cache-level intervention that keeps the model both safe and capable here suggests a broader path: treating the model's internal state as the control surface for safety, not just its inputs or its weights.

VES-RFT: Rewarding Visual Evidence Sensitivity to Mitigate Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models

The problem. Vision-language models routinely describe things that aren't in the picture — a plausible-sounding sentence that the image doesn't support. This happens because these models are, at bottom, language models bolted onto an image encoder, and language is enormously predictable on its own: once you've read "a kitchen with a stove and a," the word "refrigerator" is a good bet whether or not one is actually there. The model can score well by leaning on what sentences usually say rather than on what this particular image shows. That gap matters because it makes these systems untrustworthy exactly when we most need them to look — reading a medical scan, a legal document, a scene a robot must navigate.

The approach. Their move is to measure how much the image actually changes the model's mind, and then pay the model to be changed by it. For a given answer they run the model twice — once seeing the image, once with the image removed — and compare the uncertainty (entropy) of its word predictions in each case. If the picture genuinely informs the answer, removing it should make the model far less certain; if the answer came from language habit alone, the two look nearly identical. This per-token entropy gap is the Visual Evidence Sensitivity score. They then fine-tune the model with reinforcement learning (GRPO) using two rewards at once: the VES score, which pushes toward answers that truly depend on the image, and an ordinary correctness reward on verifiable questions, with a KL leash to the original model so nothing collapses.

What's unique. Prior hallucination fixes reward the model for being right; VES-RFT separately and directly rewards the model for using the image at all, turning "did the picture matter?" into a continuous, per-token training signal rather than treating grounding as something you only hope emerges from optimizing accuracy.

The fundamental point. The core thing it establishes is that visual grounding is measurable independently of correctness — you can quantify whether a model looked, without checking whether it was right, simply by asking how much its own uncertainty depends on the image being present. Hallucination, in this light, is not primarily a knowledge problem but an attention-allocation problem: the model's failure is that the image barely moved its predictions, and that movement is observable from the model's outputs alone, with no external labels or human judgment required (the analysis reports VES tracks human ratings of grounding).

What it implies. If "is the model actually using the image?" can be read off entropy changes, then grounding becomes a self-supervised dial you can turn during training, decoupled from the expensive, label-hungry business of factual annotation — and you can audit any deployed model the same cheap way. The assumption that falls is that reducing hallucination requires more or better correctness supervision; instead you can attack the root cause, over-reliance on language priors, directly. The honest catch, per the paper, is cost (two forward passes per sample) and the premise itself: entropy change is a proxy for grounding that breaks on questions where language priors are legitimately sufficient, so the signal is only as good as that assumption holds.

Mathematical lens

What is hidden? In VES-RFT: Rewarding Visual Evidence Sensitivity to Mitigate Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models, the method is estimating the biological or physical state behind the measurement: tissue boundary, abnormal region, cell structure, disease signal, or instrument artifact.

What counts as evidence? scanner intensities, microscope pixels, expert labels, anatomical priors, repeated measurements, and uncertainty around unclear regions.

What is the objective? infer the clinically or scientifically relevant state while respecting measurement noise, scarce labels, and domain constraints.

What breaks? a visually neat output can be scientifically wrong if it invents unsupported structure or hides uncertainty at the decision boundary.

Enhancing Part-Level Point Grounding for Any Open-Source MLLMs

The problem. Multimodal language models can point at whole objects in an image, but real robotic hands need to grab a specific part: the handle of a cup, the hinge of a laptop, the trigger of a drill. That kind of fine-grained "put the point exactly here" ability is much harder, and the obvious fix, retraining the model on part-location data, quietly breaks the very thing that made the model useful. The model overfits to the special tokens used for localization and loses its broader reasoning and language skill. So the field faces a tension: teach precise pointing without lobotomizing the model that already understands the scene.

The approach. Instead of fine-tuning the model or bolting on grounding tokens, they leave every original weight frozen and read the localization signal out of what the model is already doing internally. A small "Q-Synth" module builds grounding-aware queries from the model's own intermediate-layer activations, and an attention-to-point decoder turns the model's refined attention maps into a heatmap peaked at the target part. Supervision comes from a signed-distance penalty field that pushes probability mass toward the correct point rather than treating it as a coarse box. The whole grounding capability is added as a lightweight external head reading a frozen brain.

What's unique. Prior grounding methods inject special localization tokens and fine-tune, which is what degrades reasoning; this work extracts precise part-level points purely by synthesizing queries and refining attention on a fully frozen backbone, and it is designed to attach to any open-source MLLM rather than one specific architecture.

The fundamental point. The core thing it establishes is that the fine-grained spatial information needed for part-level pointing is already latent inside a pretrained MLLM's attention and intermediate activations, and can be decoded out without changing a single weight. Precise localization was never a missing capability that required new training, it was a readout problem: the model already "knows where," it just lacked a channel to express it as a point.

What it implies. If spatial precision is a decoding problem rather than a training problem, then the common assumption that you must fine-tune (and risk forgetting) to gain new grounding skills falls away. You can add capabilities to a frozen model through small external readers, keeping reasoning and generalization fully intact, and the same recipe can be reused across many different MLLMs instead of retraining each one, though the authors have so far mainly shown this on PACO and part-grounding, leaving open how far the "read it out, don't retrain" principle extends to other tasks and modalities.

Mathematical lens

What is hidden? In Enhancing Part-Level Point Grounding for Any Open-Source MLLMs, the method is estimating the hidden object, region, relation, or reasoning state that makes the words true in this image.

What counts as evidence? image patches, region tokens, question words, prior text knowledge, and any intermediate rationale or tool output.

What is the objective? make the answer probable only when the visual evidence and the language state support the same claim; in math terms, bind text variables to visual variables instead of letting the language prior answer alone.

What breaks? a fluent sentence can detach from the pixels, giving a confident answer whose words have no checked visual support.

Pointing at Parts: Training-Free Few-Shot Grounding in Multimodal LLMs

The problem. Machines that see and talk are now good at pointing to whole things — "that's the mug" — but bad at pointing to the pieces of a thing: the handle, the rim, the button on a screen. Parts are where most real work happens: a robot grips a handle not a mug, an editor tweaks a rim not a whole object, an inspector flags one defective seam. Parts are hard because their edges are fuzzy, they rarely have clean names, and building a labeled dataset for every part of every object is impractical. So the field is stuck: the models that can point can't point finely, and teaching them to would demand annotation nobody can afford.

The approach. Instead of training a model on part labels, POP shows it one or a few examples of the part ("here's what a handle looks like on this mug") and lets it transfer that to a new image at test time. It does this by combining two signals that already exist for free inside pretrained models. First, it reads the attention maps a multimodal LLM produces when told the word for the part — this gives a rough, language-anchored "look roughly here" region. Second, it uses a self-supervised vision encoder (DINOv3) to find which patches of the new image most resemble the example part's patches, matched in both directions to suppress false hits. Multiplying the two maps together and taking the peak yields the point: the LLM says where semantically, the visual matcher says where precisely.

What's unique. It is the first training-free method to fuse an MLLM's language-guided attention with self-supervised visual correspondence specifically for part-level pointing, and it works even on models never built to point at all (InternVL3, Kimi-VL), lifting them by up to 30.9 points to rival purpose-built pointing models.

The fundamental point. The part-pointing ability was already latent inside these models — nobody had to teach it, only extract and combine it. The paper reveals that language attention and visual similarity are complementary halves of localization: the LLM already knows the coarse semantic "where," and a generic vision encoder already knows the fine-grained "which patch," and neither alone suffices but their product does. Crucially, the capacity to point at parts does not depend on a model being trained to point — that skill can be conjured from a model that only knows how to talk about images.

What it implies. If fine-grained grounding can be assembled at inference from components pretrained models already carry, then the enormous annotation effort assumed necessary for part-level understanding is largely avoidable — a few examples replace whole labeled datasets. This decouples "can point" from "was trained to point," meaning any capable multimodal model becomes a part-grounding tool for free, and it reframes localization not as a skill to be learned but as an emergent property to be read out and fused. The remaining friction — hand-picking representative example points, and messy multi-object scenes — marks where this readout still needs a human or a better matcher, not where the idea breaks.

Mathematical lens

What is hidden? In Pointing at Parts: Training-Free Few-Shot Grounding in Multimodal LLMs, the method is estimating the population signal spread unevenly across clients, classes, labels, and unlabeled examples.

What counts as evidence? local updates, class counts, pseudo-label confidence, gradient noise, privacy clipping, and performance on rare groups.

What is the objective? combine partial evidence without pretending every client, class, or label source is equally reliable.

What breaks? naive averaging or confidence filtering can erase rare classes, leak private information, or turn unlabeled data into repeated mistakes.

DiG: Differential Grounding for Enhancing Fine-Grained Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models

The problem. Systems that fuse vision with language can describe a scene in broad strokes but stumble the moment precision matters: pointing to exactly the right object among near-identical ones, or saying precisely where something sits. This is the gap between recognizing "there is a dog" and pinning down "the third dog from the left, slightly behind the others." Closing that gap matters because most real uses of these systems, from robotics to medical reading to interface control, depend on acting on the right specific thing, not the general gist.

The approach. Instead of asking the model to localize each object in isolation, DiG teaches it to reason about the differences between regions. It sets up a comparison, contrasting the fine spatial features of candidate regions against each other so that what distinguishes near-twins becomes the signal the model attends to. Learnable spatial anchors act as reference points that steer where the model looks and what it extracts, so the differential feature comparison is anchored to concrete locations rather than floating over the whole image.

What's unique. Prior multimodal models ground objects one at a time, with no built-in machinery to hold two similar regions side by side and ask how they differ; DiG makes that relative, difference-based comparison a first-class operation and ties it to learnable anchors that direct the comparison.

The fundamental point. The core thing it reveals is that fine-grained perception is fundamentally relational, not absolute: the information that separates one object from a look-alike does not live in either region on its own but in the contrast between them. Grounding-in-isolation was quietly throwing away exactly the differential signal that distinguishing similar things requires.

What it implies. If distinctions are recoverable from comparison rather than richer per-object features, then precision in multimodal models can be improved by restructuring the reasoning to be comparative rather than by simply scaling resolution or model size. The assumption that better fine-grained perception needs ever-finer standalone features weakens, though the approach still leans on fine-grained spatial annotations and pays a computational cost for the comparison step.

Mathematical lens

What is hidden? In DiG: Differential Grounding for Enhancing Fine-Grained Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models, the method is estimating the biological or physical state behind the measurement: tissue boundary, abnormal region, cell structure, disease signal, or instrument artifact.

What counts as evidence? scanner intensities, microscope pixels, expert labels, anatomical priors, repeated measurements, and uncertainty around unclear regions.

What is the objective? infer the clinically or scientifically relevant state while respecting measurement noise, scarce labels, and domain constraints.

What breaks? a visually neat output can be scientifically wrong if it invents unsupported structure or hides uncertainty at the decision boundary.

GroundingME: Exposing the Visual Grounding Gap in MLLMs through Multi-Dimensional Evaluation

The problem. When you tell a machine "point to the object I mean," it has to connect a phrase to an actual place in an image — the skill that lets a robot pick up "the mug behind the kettle" instead of any mug. Today's multimodal models score near-perfect on the standard tests for this, which has quietly created the impression that the problem is solved. But those tests mostly ask for easy, unambiguous objects in clean scenes. The gap between "aces the test" and "can be trusted to act in a cluttered real room" is exactly where safety-critical uses like robotic instruction live, and nobody had a clear measurement of how wide that gap actually is.

The approach. The authors build GroundingME, a deliberately hard set of 1,005 hand-refined image-description pairs, and organize it around four things real grounding demands rather than one blanket score. It probes whether a model can tell near-identical objects apart (Discriminative), follow layered spatial relationships (Spatial), find things that are occluded or tiny (Limited), and — crucially — refuse to point at something the description does not actually match (Rejection). They then run 25 leading models through it and test two fixes: letting a model "think" step-by-step before answering, and blending rejection examples into training.

What's unique. Prior benchmarks reward a single localization number on mostly groundable, well-separated objects. GroundingME instead decomposes grounding into four failure-prone axes with twelve diagnostic subcategories, and — most distinctively — makes the ability to say "that is not here" a first-class scored dimension rather than assuming every query has an answer.

The fundamental point. The core reveal is that near-perfect scores on existing grounding benchmarks were an artifact of the benchmarks, not evidence of the skill: the best of 25 top models reaches only 45.1% here, and most score 0% on rejection. That last number is the deeper finding — current models have essentially no capacity to recognize that a described object is absent; they will confidently ground a phrase onto whatever is nearest, because they were only ever trained and tested on the assumption that a correct target always exists.

What it implies. If grounding is really four separable abilities and today's models are missing most of the hard ones — especially the reflex to abstain — then a high grounding score cannot be read as readiness for a robot to act on it, and "always answer" is a dangerous default in the physical world. The encouraging half is that abstention is teachable rather than fundamental: mixing in rejection data moved a model from 0% to 27.9%, showing the gap is a training-objective blind spot, not a hard ceiling. Closing it means evaluating and training for refusal and fine-grained discrimination explicitly, not hoping they emerge from scaling on easy data.

Mathematical lens

What is hidden? In GroundingME: Exposing the Visual Grounding Gap in MLLMs through Multi-Dimensional Evaluation, the method is estimating how much support the evidence really gives the prediction, especially when the input is shifted, ambiguous, rare, or risky.

What counts as evidence? confidence scores, disagreement, ensembles or samples, residual error, domain shift, and downstream cost of being wrong.

What is the objective? separate what is known from what is guessed, so probability means calibrated belief rather than decorative confidence.

What breaks? the most dangerous error is a wrong answer that stays confident, because no later system knows to slow down or ask for help.
