Dataset Distillation by Influence Matching ⌘

The problem. Modern models are trained on enormous datasets that are slow, expensive, and largely redundant. Dataset distillation asks whether a handful of carefully manufactured synthetic images can stand in for millions of real ones, letting a model trained on the tiny set behave as if it saw the whole thing. The catch is that most distillation methods overfit to the exact recipe used to make them: the tiny set works for one architecture on one task but loses its meaning and stops transferring the moment you change the model or the goal.

The approach. Instead of forcing the synthetic images to reproduce the appearance of real data or the final trained weights, they match how the data acts on learning. Influence functions measure how much each training example bends a model's gradients and outcomes, effectively each sample's causal footprint on what the model becomes. They synthesize a small set whose collective influence pattern mirrors that of the full dataset, so a model trained on the distilled set is steered along the same learning trajectory. The synthetic samples are optimized until their influence signature, not their pixels, matches the original.

What's unique. Prior distillation matched surface-level proxies, gradients, features, or training trajectories, tied to a specific network. This is the first method to make the matching target the influence function itself, which captures each sample's effect on learning in an architecture-agnostic way, and it comes with a theoretical justification rather than a purely empirical recipe.

The fundamental point. It reveals that the transferable essence of a dataset is not its images or even its statistics, but its influence structure, how its examples collectively push a model as it learns. What a dataset is for training purposes can be reduced to this footprint on the learning process, and that footprint is largely independent of which model or task consumes it.

What it implies. If a dataset's value lives in its influence pattern rather than its pixels, then distilled sets can be built once and reused across architectures and tasks, breaking the one-model-one-distillation lock-in that limited the field. It reframes distillation as preserving learning dynamics rather than copying data, though it inherits the open cost of computing influence at scale, which is why ImageNet-scale use still needs work.

Mathematical lens

What is hidden? In Dataset Distillation by Influence Matching, the method is estimating the small subspace, token set, or behavior pattern that carries most of the useful computation.

What counts as evidence? teacher probabilities, feature similarity, ranks, token saliency, latency, memory, and accuracy under compression.

What is the objective? approximate the original behavior with fewer parameters, tokens, bits, or operations while bounding the loss that matters.

What breaks? a cheaper model may preserve average accuracy while losing rare behavior, calibration, long-range context, or the teacher's useful uncertainty.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

ProxyFL: A Proxy-Guided Framework for Federated Semi-Supervised Learning ⌘

The problem. Imagine training one shared model across thousands of phones or hospitals that can't pool their raw data. Two mismatches sabotage this. Across sites, each holds a skewed slice of the world (one clinic sees mostly one disease, another sees others), so the local models pull in conflicting directions. Within a site, only a sliver of data is labeled while most is not, so each site is trying to learn from mostly unnamed examples. Getting this right matters because the data worth learning from increasingly lives on private devices where labels are scarce and centralizing everything is either illegal or impossible.

The approach. Instead of shipping around whole models or hand-crafting clever ways to average them, ProxyFL treats the classifier's weights as a compact stand-in ("proxy") for what categories exist and in what proportions, both at each site and globally. A Global Proxy-Tuning step explicitly optimizes a shared proxy to match the true category distribution spread across all sites, correcting the bias you get from naive averaging. For the unlabeled data, instead of forcing a confident-but-often-wrong single guess and discarding the rest, its Indecisive-Categories Proxy Learning lets an uncertain example declare a small set of plausible categories, then anchors it to labeled examples through a relationship pool so every sample, even the ambiguous ones, contributes to training.

What's unique. Prior work attacked the two heterogeneities separately, with elaborate aggregation schemes or by throwing away low-confidence samples. ProxyFL is the first to use a single lightweight mechanism, the classifier weights as a category proxy, to address both the cross-site distribution gap and the within-site labeled/unlabeled gap at once, adding no extra privacy exposure or communication overhead.

The fundamental point. The core insight is that the classifier's own weights already encode a distribution over categories, so heterogeneity, whether between sites or between labeled and unlabeled data within a site, is fundamentally the same problem: a distribution mismatch that can be read off and corrected in this proxy space. It also establishes that a low-confidence sample was never useless; the information loss came from collapsing it to one label, and keeping it as a set of candidates recovers that signal.

What it implies. If both heterogeneities reduce to distribution mismatch in one shared representation, then the field can stop building separate, ever-more-complex machinery for each and instead correct them jointly and cheaply. And if uncertain data can be kept in the training rather than filtered out, the common assumption that federated semi-supervised learning must sacrifice most of its data to confidence thresholds falls away, which matters most exactly where labels are scarcest and heterogeneity is worst.

Mathematical lens

What is hidden? In ProxyFL: A Proxy-Guided Framework for Federated Semi-Supervised Learning, the method is estimating the population signal spread unevenly across clients, classes, labels, and unlabeled examples.

What counts as evidence? local updates, class counts, pseudo-label confidence, gradient noise, privacy clipping, and performance on rare groups.

What is the objective? combine partial evidence without pretending every client, class, or label source is equally reliable.

What breaks? naive averaging or confidence filtering can erase rare classes, leak private information, or turn unlabeled data into repeated mistakes.
